Mastery
măs´tẽr-ĭ
n. (dominion, victory; the contest of the games — Greek agonizomai, to strive in the arena)
From master, Latin magister. In 1 Corinthians 9:25 the phrase striveth for the mastery renders a single Greek verb drawn from the athletic contests.

Biblical Definition

Mastery is dominion won in a contest, and Paul takes the word from the games: “every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible” (1Co 9:25). He is arguing from what everyone in Corinth had seen at the Isthmian games. An athlete in training governs his sleep, his food, and his company, not because those things are wicked but because he is after a prize; and he does it for a wreath that withers. Paul applies it to himself without flinching: “I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway” (1Co 9:27). The word appears elsewhere in its plain senses. On the mountain Moses corrects Joshua's reading of the noise below: “It is not the voice of them that shout for mastery, neither is it the voice of them that cry for being overcome: but the noise of them that sing do I hear” (Exo 32:18) — not a battle, but a revel around a calf. And in the lions' den, of Daniel's accusers: “the lions had the mastery of them, and brake all their bones in pieces or ever they came at the bottom of the den” (Dan 6:24), the same lions that had not touched Daniel.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines mastery as dominion; power of command; superiority; pre-eminence; victory in war or in a contest.

expand to see more

MAS'TERY, n. Dominion; power of governing or commanding.

2. Superiority in competition; preeminence; victory in war or in a contest.

3. Superior dexterity; superior skill; as, to obtain the mastery of an art.

TEM'PERATE, a. Moderate; not excessive; governing the appetites and passions.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 9:25 — "And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible."

1 Corinthians 9:27 — "But I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway."

Exodus 32:18 — "And he said, It is not the voice of them that shout for mastery, neither is it the voice of them that cry for being overcome: but the noise of them that sing do I hear."

Daniel 6:24 — "And the king commanded, and they brought those men which had accused Daniel, and they cast them into the den of lions, them, their children, and their wives; and the lions had the mastery of them, and brake all their bones in pieces or ever they came at the bottom of the den."

Modern Corruption

Discipline of the body is dismissed as legalism, and Paul's own practice — keeping under his body lest he be a castaway — is explained away rather than imitated.

expand to see more

A generation that has rightly learned that works do not justify has often wrongly concluded that effort is suspect. First Corinthians 9 is written by the apostle of justification by faith, and it is full of running, striving, buffeting and subjection. The distinction is not difficult: no exertion earns a standing before God, and no man who has that standing is thereby excused from training. Paul draws his illustration from athletes who were temperate in all things for a wreath that browned in a week, and asks the obvious question about a crown that does not fade. Where self-denial is treated as legalism by definition, the church loses the very vocabulary this chapter supplies.

Verse 27 is the sharpest and the most argued over: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway. It does not teach that a true believer may perish, which the same apostle denies at length in Romans 8; it teaches that the means by which God keeps His people include their striving, and that a preacher is not exempt from the warnings he administers. The doctrine of perseverance is a doctrine of perseverance — the saints are kept, and they are kept persevering. A man who reasons from his security to his slackness has not understood the security.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek agonizomai (G75), to contend in the games, strive for the mastery — 1 Corinthians 9:25, Colossians 1:29, 1 Timothy 6:12; enkrateuomai (G1467), to be temperate; Hebrew gaburah (H1369), might, mastery.

expand to see more

Greek agonizomai (G75) — to strive as in the arena; 1 Corinthians 9:25, Luke 13:24, Colossians 4:12 of Epaphras labouring fervently in prayer.

Greek enkrateuomai (G1467) — to exercise self-control, be temperate; 1 Corinthians 9:25 and 7:9.

Greek adokimos (G96) — disapproved, castaway; 1 Corinthians 9:27, the athlete disqualified.

Hebrew gaburah (H1369) — might, mastery; Exodus 32:18, of the shout of the strong.

The Isthmian games were held near Corinth, so Paul's readers knew exactly what training he meant.

Usage

"“Every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things”."

"“They do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible”."

"“The lions had the mastery of them” — the same lions that had not touched Daniel."
